summary: Defines Uniform Resource Locators for Z39.50, an information retrieval protocol that works in sessions with multiple steps rather than one-shot fetches. It lets you link to Z39.50 resources.

plainLanguage.summary: This gives a web address to a library catalogue search so you can link to it like a web page.

questions: how to link to a z39.50 database
what is the default z39.50 port
subtitle: Two URL schemes that let a link open a Z39.50 library-search session or fetch one specific record.

tldr.problem: Z39.50 is a session-oriented, multi-step information retrieval protocol, so it does not fit a URL model built around the stateless fetch of data.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two schemes, z39.50s for a Session URL that opens an interactive client session and z39.50r for a Retrieval URL that fetches a single known record using a document identifier.
tldr.outcome: Z39.50 resources can be linked to like other URLs, and the scheme itself tells the user interface whether a session or a one-off retrieval is meant.

today: The record lists RFC 2056 as a Proposed Standard, and no obsoleting or updating RFC is recorded for it.

sections.title: Why Z39.50 Needs Two URL Schemes
sections.content:
Z39.50 is an information retrieval protocol. It models a user inquiry as a session-oriented, multi-step task, and any step may be suspended while the server asks the client for more parameters. That does not fit a retrieval model designed around the stateless fetch of data.

Retrieval of well-known data can still be done in one step, as a degenerate session of exactly one search request and response. Two core functions emerge, handled by two URL schemes: the Session URL and the Retrieval URL.

Making the distinction at the scheme level lets the user interface show it to the user without parsing otherwise opaque parts of the URL.
sections.plainLanguage: Some links should open a library search for you to play with, and others should just fetch one item. Two kinds of address make that clear before you click.

sections.title: Basic Z39.50 Concepts
sections.content:
The two most basic operations are Search and Present. In a Search, the client gives search criteria and names one or more databases on the server. The result is a result set of pointers to the selected database records. Through Present, the client then asks for a retrieval record.

The URL uses four terms. The database is what is searched. The elementset says which elements of the record are wanted. The recordsyntax says how the retrieval record is packaged. The docid is a document identifier used in a known-item search, where the client wants a single known record.
sections.plainLanguage: You pick a shelf (the database), say which parts of a book card you want, choose how the card is printed, and give the book's ID number.

sections.title: The Session URL (z39.50s)
sections.content:
The Session URL switches the user to a Z39.50 client application. The host is required. The port is optional and defaults to 210. All other parameters are optional, but a database must be included if a docid is included.

The client starts a session to the host and port, or may reuse an already open session to the same host and port. If a docid is given, the client performs the specified search as for the Retrieval URL. If not, any other parameters are only hints, which clients may treat as requirements, as preferences, or ignore.

In every case the client leaves the session open for the user to do retrievals and new searches. That is the main distinction from the Retrieval URL.
sections.plainLanguage: A session link opens the library's search desk and keeps it open so you can keep searching.

sections.title: The Retrieval URL (z39.50r)
sections.content:
The Retrieval URL uses a Z39.50 session as a transparent transfer mechanism to retrieve one specific information object. The client builds a Search Request from the URL. If the number of matching records does not equal one, the retrieval is unsuccessful and the client's behavior is not defined. If exactly one record matches, the server may include it in the Search Response; if not, the client asks for it with a Present Request. Afterwards it may close the session or keep it open.

The host and a database are required, and the port defaults to 210. A Retrieval URL with no docid has an undefined meaning. The docid is put into a type-1 query as the single term, in the general format (tag 45), using the Bib-1 attribute set, with a Use attribute value of docid and a structure attribute of URx. The docid string is server-defined and completely opaque to the client.

If esn is given, it should be used in the Search request or in a following Present request. If rs lists record syntaxes, the client should pick one, preferably the first it supports, as the PreferredRecordSyntax. Without them, the choice is the client's.
sections.plainLanguage: A retrieval link walks up, asks for exactly one item by its ID, takes it and may leave. If the ID matches zero or many items, the link does not say what happens.

sections.title: URL Syntax
sections.content:
Both schemes follow the Common Internet Scheme Syntax of RFC 1738. The scheme name is z39.50r or z39.50s, followed by ://, the host and an optional port. After a / come one or more databases joined by +, an optional ? and docid, an optional ;esn= element set and an optional ;rs= list of record syntaxes joined by +.

Future extensions are to take the form ;keyword=value. The RFC also copies the character-class definitions from RFC 1738 and notes two changes made between the Internet Draft and RFC 1738: = moved from extra to reserved, and national was removed from unreserved.
sections.plainLanguage: The address has a fixed order of parts, like a street address, and extra settings are added at the end after semicolons.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The appendix gives three examples. A session URL for the MELVYL union catalog "cat" at the University of California is z39.50s://melvyl.ucop.edu/cat.

A retrieval URL that opens the MELVYL magazine database just long enough to fetch an article is z39.50r://melvyl.ucop.edu/mags?elecworld.v30.n19. The part after the ? is determined by the server.

A third, z39.50r://cnidr.org:2100/tmf?bkirch_rules__a1;esn=f;rs=marc, asks for a full record (element set "f") in the MARC syntax from a hypothetical database called TMF, on the non-standard port 2100.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show a link that opens a catalogue, a link that grabs one magazine article, and a link that asks for a full card in a particular format.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The two schemes carry the same security implications as the general URL scheme in RFC 1738, so the usual precautions apply. A locator might no longer point to the object originally intended.

It may also be possible to build a URL so that an attempt at a harmless idempotent operation, such as retrieving an object, causes a possibly damaging remote operation.
sections.plainLanguage: A link can go stale, and a sneaky link might make something happen that you did not expect, so be careful what you click.
